files.lesson.md: --- order: 1 unit: exponentials node: AC9M10A03 n1 uses: [AC9M8N02 n1] # powers: 2⁴ = 16 connection: food-left-out title: Same ratio each time summary: "A table that adds the same amount each step is linear. A table that multiplies by the same number each step is exponential, and its last steps add far more than its first." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Leave a sandwich out and the germs on it multiply. Why does the food rule change at 2 hours, and bin it at 4?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8390 url: http://127.0.0.1:8390/index.html readySelector: "#sl-b" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: ratio.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Both lines start at 100 and reach 200 after one half hour. The solid line doubles each time; the dashed line adds 100." } explainClip: query: { code: "@ratio.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Adding and multiplying start together, then split apart" say: "Adding and multiplying start together, then they split apart." clip: - caption: { text: "The dashed line adds 100 every half hour.", say: "The dashed line adds one hundred every half hour." } - wait: 600 - click: Make b bigger - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Now the solid line doubles every half hour.", say: "Now the solid line doubles every half hour." } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Same start, same first step. Then it runs away.", say: "Same start and same first step, and then it runs away." } - wait: 1200 --- At a picnic, a sandwich sits on the table. The food safety rule goes like this: under 2 hours, eat it or put it back in the fridge. From 2 to 4 hours, eat it, but don't put it back. At 4 hours or more, throw it out ([the 2-hour/4-hour rule, NSW Food Authority](https://www.foodauthority.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-07/2_hour_4_hour_rule.pdf)). To see why the rule changes the way it does, let's pretend the germs on the sandwich double every half hour, starting from 100. That's made up: real doubling times depend on the germs and the temperature. ## Predict: the sandwich at 4 hours ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a germ count at 4 hours shows who thinks twice as long means twice as many (3,200) and who sees that each half hour doubles the one before." check: type: predict q: "After 2 hours there are 1,600 germs. The germs keep doubling every half hour. How many are there after 4 hours?" options: - "$25{,}600$" - "$12{,}800$" - "$6{,}400$" - "$3{,}200$" actual: "25,600. From 2 hours to 4 hours is 4 more half hours, so the count doubles 4 more times: 1,600 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 25,600. That is 16 times as many, not twice as many." ``` The bars show the germs on the sandwich for the first 2 hours. Make a guess before you check. ## Run: add or multiply ```step stage: run insight: "Adding 100 each half hour and doubling each half hour agree for the first step and then split apart: the multiplying line runs away." try: { playground: board, starter: "ratio.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $b$ to 2, so the germs double each half hour. Read the table at 2 hours ($x = 4$) and 4 hours ($x = 8$). Was your prediction right?", when: "b = 2" } ``` The solid line multiplies by $b$ every half hour. The dashed line just adds 100 every half hour. The chart runs out of room, so read the big numbers from the table. ## Investigate: ratio, not difference ```step stage: investigate insight: "An exponential table has a constant ratio between neighbours, not a constant difference. Priya checks the differences, which is the test for a linear table." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A table goes $5, 15, 45, 135$. What do you multiply by to get from each value to the next?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["10", "10 is how far it goes up from 5 to 15. The ratio is what you multiply by: 15 ÷ 5."] - ["30", "30 is how far it goes up from 15 to 45. What do you multiply 15 by to get 45?"] explain: "15 ÷ 5 = 3, 45 ÷ 15 = 3 and 135 ÷ 45 = 3. Each value is 3 times the one before." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#priya" text: "Priya tests the table $3, 6, 12, 24$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: exp-test-difference explain: "Line 2: exponential doesn't mean 'goes up by the same amount'. That's a linear table. Exponential means multiplying by the same number: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 24 ÷ 12 = 2, so this table is exponential." - check: type: question q: "Which of these tables is exponential?" options: ["$2, 5, 8, 11$", "$2, 6, 18, 54$", "$2, 4, 8, 14$"] answer: 1 feedback: ["That adds 3 every time. It's a linear table.", null, "2, 4, 8 doubles, but 8 to 14 only adds 6 (14 ÷ 8 is 1.75). The ratio isn't the same every step."] explain: "2, 6, 18, 54 multiplies by 3 every time: 6 ÷ 2, 18 ÷ 6 and 54 ÷ 18 are all 3." ``` ### Multiply by what? Here's how to tell the two kinds of table apart. ```worked 2,\; 6,\; 18,\; 54 :: Is this table linear or exponential? 6 - 2 = 4,\; 18 - 6 = 12,\; 54 - 18 = 36 :: The differences are 4, 12, 36. They aren't the same, so it isn't linear. 6 \div 2 = 3,\; 18 \div 6 = 3,\; 54 \div 18 = 3 :: Divide each value by the one before. Every time, it's 3. \text{ratio} = 3 :: A constant ratio means exponential: each value is 3 times the one before. 54 \times 3 = 162 :: So the next value is 162. ``` Now try one on paper like the example: $5, 15, 45, 135$. Find the ratio, then type it. ### Find the mistake Read Priya's working. What does 'exponential' mean for a table? ### Which table? Check the ratio for each one. ## Modify: change the ratio ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a bigger ratio, a ratio below 1 (the numbers fall), and a ratio of exactly 1 (nothing changes)." try: { playground: board, starter: "ratio.yml#vary", height: 640 } tasks: - hint: ["Set $b$ to 3.", "The count at 2 hours is the table value at $x = 4$."] check: { type: answer, q: "Set $b$ to 3, so the germs triple every half hour. How many germs are there after 2 hours ($x = 4$)?", answer: "8100", feedback: [["1200", "That's 100 × 3 × 4. Tripling four times means × 3 four times: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81."], ["400", "That's 100 × 4. Tripling means × 3, and it happens four times."]], explain: "100 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 100 × 81 = 8,100." } - hint: "Set $b$ to 0.5. Is each value still a fixed multiple of the one before?" check: type: question q: "Set $b$ to 0.5. The numbers get smaller each step. Is it still an exponential table?" options: ["Yes: each value is 0.5 times the one before, so the ratio is still the same every step", "No: exponential tables only go up", "No: the ratio has to be a whole number"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A ratio below 1 makes the numbers fall. Each value is half the one before, and that's still a constant ratio.", "A ratio can be a fraction or a decimal. 0.5 is the same as ÷ 2."] explain: "A constant ratio is all it takes. With b = 0.5 each value is half the one before: 100, 50, 25, 12.5..." - hint: "Set $b$ to 1 and look at the table." check: type: question q: "Edge case: set $b$ to 1. The values stay at 100. What are the difference and the ratio between neighbours?" options: ["The difference is 0 and the ratio is 1: both are the same every step", "The difference is 1 and the ratio is 0", "The difference is 0 and the ratio is 0"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Swapped: nothing is added, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing.", "Multiplying by 0 would make every value 0. The ratio here is 1."] explain: "100 + 0 = 100 and 100 × 1 = 100. A ratio of 1 means nothing changes, so it's a flat line." ``` ### Triple Each task changes $b$. Set the board, then answer. ### A ratio below 1 ### A ratio of 1 ## Practise: find the ratio ```step stage: practise insight: "Finding a ratio, using it to go on, telling linear from exponential, and (review) reading what a line adds." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "The table goes $6, 18, 54, 162$. What comes next?" answer: "486" feedback: - ["216", "216 is 162 + 54, the last difference added on. An exponential table multiplies: 162 × 3."] - ["324", "324 is 162 × 2. What do you multiply by each time here?"] explain: "18 ÷ 6 = 3, so each value is 3 times the one before: 162 × 3 = 486." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Just one step: how many times bigger is 18 than 6?", answer: 3, explain: "18 ÷ 6 = 3. Check it against 54 ÷ 18." } - check: type: answer q: "The table goes $80, 40, 20, 10$. What do you multiply by each time?" answer: "0.5" feedback: - ["2", "Going from 80 to 40 makes it smaller. Multiply by 2 would make it bigger."] - ["-40", "That's 40 − 80. The ratio is what you multiply by: 40 ÷ 80."] explain: "40 ÷ 80 = 0.5, and 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. Each value is half the one before." - check: type: question q: "Which table is exponential?" options: ["$5, 11, 17, 23$", "$5, 10, 20, 40$", "$5, 10, 15, 25$"] answer: 1 feedback: ["That adds 6 every time. It's linear.", null, "5, 10, 15 adds 5, but then 15 to 25 adds 10. It's neither."] explain: "5, 10, 20, 40 multiplies by 2 every time." - check: type: answer q: "Review: the line $y = 3x + 2$. How much does $y$ go up each time $x$ goes up by 1?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["2", "2 is where the line crosses the y-axis. Look at the number in front of x."] explain: "m = 3: a line adds the same amount each step. That's the difference between a line and an exponential." ``` ### Next value ### Decay ### Which one? ### Review Straight lines, from Linear relations. ## Make: back to the sandwich ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the picnic: the doubling model says 4 hours is 16 times as many germs as 2 hours, not twice as many." tasks: - hint: ["2 hours is 4 half-hours; 4 hours is 8 half-hours.", "Start from 100 and double that many times."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The sandwich starts with 100 germs and they double every half hour. How many times as many germs are there after 4 hours as after 2 hours?" steps: - ["2 hours is 4 half-hours: $100 \\times 2^4 = 1600$ germs", "double 4 times"] - ["4 hours is 8 half-hours: $100 \\times 2^8 = 25600$ germs", "double 8 times"] - ["$25600 \\div 1600 = 16$", "how many times as many"] answer: "16" answerLabel: "Times as many" feedback: - ["2", "4 hours is twice as long as 2 hours, but the germs double 4 more times, not once."] - ["8", "There are 4 extra doublings: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16."] criteria: - "I worked out the germs at 2 hours and at 4 hours." - "I used doubling, not adding." - "My answer is a lot more than 2." explain: "1,600 at 2 hours and 25,600 at 4 hours. 25,600 ÷ 1,600 = 16 times as many." - check: type: question q: "A friend says: 'The rule throws the food out at 4 hours, but 4 is only double 2, so it's only twice as risky.' In the doubling model, what's wrong with that?" options: ["Doubling every half hour means 4 hours has 16 times the germs of 2 hours, not 2 times", "Nothing: twice as long means twice as many germs", "4 hours has 8 times the germs of 2 hours"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That's what an adding table does. These germs multiply, so the last hours add the most.", "That would be only 3 extra doublings. From 2 hours to 4 hours is 4 half-hours."] explain: "Each half hour doubles the count, so the extra 2 hours double it 4 times: 16 times as many." ``` ### 4 hours against 2 Back to the picnic. Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Twice as risky? The rule's numbers come from food scientists, and the model here is made up. But the shape is the point: with multiplying, the last hours add far more than the first. Sources: the 2-hour/4-hour rule is from [NSW Food Authority](https://www.foodauthority.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-07/2_hour_4_hour_rule.pdf). The 100 germs and the doubling every half hour are made up for this lesson. **Also used in** - **Money.** Savings that earn the same percentage each year multiply, so the last years add the most. - **Sharing.** A post that everyone who sees it sends to 3 friends: each round multiplies. - **Next lessons.** The graph of a multiplying table, then its rule, then solving for when it reaches a number. ```teacher summary: Students compare a table that adds with one that multiplies on a graph board, find the constant ratio, tell the two kinds of table apart, and use the doubling model to see why the last hours of a food-safety rule matter most (AC9M10A03, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can tell a table that adds from a table that multiplies. - I can find the ratio of an exponential table. - I can explain why doubling 4 times is not the same as doubling once. struggle: Checking differences instead of ratios. Ask 'what do I do to this number to get the next one?', adding or multiplying, before any dividing. before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. Students need powers from Year 8 (2⁴ = 16) and straight-line tables from Linear relations. The one idea: an exponential table has a constant ratio between neighbours, where a linear table has a constant difference. The board puts both on one graph: they agree for the first step (100 to 200) and then split. That is the picture to come back to. All numbers in the germ model are made up: 100 germs at the start, doubling every half hour. Say so in class. Real doubling times depend on the germs and the temperature, and the food rule's cut-offs come from food-safety research, not from this model. The model only shows the shape: why 'twice as long' is not 'twice as much' when things multiply. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 3,200 are adding or thinking 'twice as long, twice as many'. Don't correct it yet." - "Run: ask students to read the two rows of the table at 2 hours and at 4 hours, and say what the dashed row is doing." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the picnic in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for division (ratio), not subtraction." - "Modify: before the ratio of 1, ask what multiplying by 1 does." stuck: - see: A student checks the differences to see if a table is exponential (Priya's mistake). ask: "What do you do to 3 to get 6, and to 6 to get 12: add or multiply?" fix: "Write ÷ under each arrow: 6 ÷ 3, 12 ÷ 6, 24 ÷ 12. Differences test a line; ratios test an exponential." - see: A student says 4 hours is only twice as bad as 2 hours. ask: How many half-hours is 2 hours? And 4 hours? How many extra doublings is that? fix: "Count the doublings: 4 for the first 2 hours, 4 more for the next 2. Four more doublings is × 16." - see: A student thinks a falling table (80, 40, 20, 10) can't be exponential. ask: What do you multiply 80 by to get 40? fix: Multiply by 0.5 each time. A ratio below 1 is still a constant ratio. stretch: "Find a ratio that makes the germs reach 10,000 after 3 half-hours from 100. Is it a whole number? Then: can an exponential table ever be the same as a linear one? (Only with ratio 1.)" support: "A table with an extra row for each step: '+?' on one row and '×?' on the next. Fill both for 2, 4, 8, 16 and for 2, 4, 6, 8 so the contrast is visible." leads: > Next: the graph of an exponential (y-intercept, growth or decay, the line it never reaches), then reading the rule y = a(bˣ) from a graph, then solving equations where x is the power. Where it leads in class: compound interest and depreciation (the same percentage each year), and half-life in science. exit: q: A table goes 3, 12, 48, 192. Is it linear or exponential? What is the next value? a: "Exponential: each value is 4 times the one before. The next value is 768." explain: > A table is **exponential** when each value is the same number of times the one before. That number is the **ratio**: divide a value by the one before it. A linear table has a constant **difference** instead: the same amount added each step. $5, 10, 15, 20$ is linear. $5, 10, 20, 40$ is exponential, with ratio 2. A ratio below 1 is still exponential: $80, 40, 20, 10$ has ratio 0.5. sources: - title: "The 2-hour/4-hour rule (NSW Food Authority): under 2 hours use or refrigerate, 2 to 4 hours use but don't refrigerate, 4 hours or more throw out (food held between 5 °C and 60 °C)" url: https://www.foodauthority.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-07/2_hour_4_hour_rule.pdf checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Boards for "Same ratio each time". x counts half-hours, so x = 4 is 2 hours and x = 8 is 4 hours.
# The solid line multiplies by b each half hour; the dashed line adds 100 each half hour. Both start at 100.
# The made-up numbers (100 germs, doubling every half hour) are labelled as made up in the lesson.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: 0, 8
y: 0, 1600
grid: 1, 400
axes: Time (half-hours), Germs
slider b: 1, 3, 1
plot: y = 100(b^x)
plot: y = 100 + 100x, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: 0, 8
y: 0, 1600
grid: 1, 400
axes: Time (half-hours), Germs
slider b: 1, 3, 1
plot: y = 100(b^x)
plot: y = 100 + 100x, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: 0, 8
y: 0, 1600
grid: 1, 400
axes: Time (half-hours), Germs
plot: y = 100(2^x)
plot: y = 100 + 100x, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: graph
x: 0, 8
y: 0, 1600
grid: 1, 400
axes: Time (half-hours), Germs
slider b: 0.5, 3, 2, 0.5
plot: y = 100(b^x)
plot: y = 100 + 100x, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
# endregion

# Priya's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: priya
Is the table 3, 6, 12, 24 exponential?
Exponential means it goes up by the same amount each step, so I'll check the differences.
6 − 3 = 3, 12 − 6 = 6, 24 − 12 = 12. The differences aren't the same.
So the table isn't exponential.
# endregion
